summary: The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco, traditionally in 1325, and served the Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco until they overthrew them in 1428 and formed the Triple Alliance with Texcoco and Tlacopan. Under Itzcoatl, Moctezuma I, Axayacatl and Ahuitzotl the alliance built a tributary empire across central Mexico to the Gulf, Oaxaca and Soconusco, though it was halted by the Purépecha in the west. Cortés arrived in 1519 with Indigenous allies; after smallpox and a long siege, Tenochtitlan fell on 13 August 1521, after the map ends.

details: The Mexica had settled on an island in Lake Texcoco, in the Valley of Mexico, where they founded Tenochtitlan, traditionally in 1325. It was a small city paying tribute to the powerful Tepanec city of Azcapotzalco. After the death of their leader Tenoch, the elders chose a king with prestigious connections: Acamapichtli, a noble from Culhuacan whose rulers claimed descent from the ancient Toltecs. He became the first tlatoani (king) of Tenochtitlan and founded its royal dynasty. The chronicles disagree on his dates, placing the start of his reign between 1350 and 1376.

For decades Tenochtitlan fought as a junior ally of Azcapotzalco, helping it build a tributary empire. When the Tepanec king Tezozomoc died in 1426, his son Maxtla seized power, turned on the Mexica and blockaded their city, and their king Chimalpopoca died, possibly murdered. The new Mexica king Itzcoatl allied with Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco, the city of Tlacopan and Huexotzinco. Together they defeated Azcapotzalco in 1428. Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan formed the Triple Alliance, and the Aztec Empire begins on the map.

Moctezuma I, a nephew of Itzcoatl, had been one of his leading generals and was chosen as ruler on Itzcoatl's death in 1440. Early in his reign he conquered Oaxaca, and he went on to push the empire beyond the Valley of Mexico to the Gulf Coast for the first time, subduing the Huastec and Totonac peoples. This brought luxury goods such as cacao, rubber, cotton and feathers to Tenochtitlan as tribute. He also faced frost, drought and severe famine in the 1450s. By his death in 1469, the empire stretched from the Gulf toward the Pacific.

The Toluca Valley, west of the Valley of Mexico, was home to the Matlatzinca people and lay on the frontier with the Purépecha (Tarascan) Empire of Michoacán, the Aztecs' great western rival. According to the Aztec Empire article, the Purépecha had invaded the valley in 1455. Axayacatl, Moctezuma I's successor, retook it in 1472 and held it against Purépecha counterattacks. The article on Axayacatl dates his Toluca campaign to 1474. The valley became the Aztecs' heavily defended western frontier.

Encouraged by his success in the Toluca Valley, Axayacatl launched a major invasion of the Purépecha Empire. According to the Aztec Empire article, in 1479 he led 32,000 soldiers into Michoacán and met a Purépecha army of 50,000 just across the border, which killed or captured over 90% of his force. The article on Axayacatl dates the defeat to 1476. Axayacatl was wounded and never fought the Purépecha again. It was the Aztecs' first major defeat, and the Purépecha frontier, fortified afterwards, permanently blocked Aztec expansion to the west.

After Axayacatl's brother Tizoc died, probably murdered by his own nobles, another brother, Ahuitzotl, took power in 1486. He first crushed rebellions, then launched a great wave of conquests. His armies took the Oaxaca Valley, conquered Mixtec and Zapotec peoples and pushed down the Pacific coast as far as Soconusco, near today's border with Guatemala. He also rebuilt the Templo Mayor, the great temple of Tenochtitlan, on a grander scale in 1487. Under Ahuitzotl the Aztec Empire reached close to its greatest extent on the map.

When Ahuitzotl died in 1502, his nephew Moctezuma II, son of Axayacatl, was chosen as ruler. He set out to centralise power, creating new provinces and replacing many of his predecessors' advisers. He also widened the gap between nobles and commoners, barring commoners from serving in the royal palace or high office. He continued campaigns of conquest early in his reign and fought 'flower wars' against Tlaxcala, the Aztecs' unconquered enemy to the east. The empire was at its height, but many subject peoples resented its heavy tribute.

The Purépecha Empire to the west remained undefeated since Axayacatl's disaster decades earlier, and border clashes continued. In 1515 Aztec armies commanded by the Tlaxcalan general Tlahuicole invaded Purépecha territory again. They failed to take any land and were mostly limited to raiding, and the Purépecha defeated them and forced them to withdraw. The western frontier stayed where it was. Just four years later, Spanish ships would appear on the Gulf coast.

In 1519 the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés sailed from Cuba with a small expedition. In April he landed on the Gulf coast, where he founded the settlement of Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz and allied with the Totonac city of Cempoala. With the help of his interpreter, La Malinche, he gathered indigenous allies, above all the Tlaxcalans, who were the Aztecs' bitter enemies. On 8 November 1519 he entered Tenochtitlan and met Moctezuma II. Soon afterwards he took the emperor captive in his own city.

In May 1520 the Spaniard Pedro de Alvarado massacred Aztec nobles during the festival of Toxcatl, and the city rose against the Spaniards. In late June Moctezuma died in unclear circumstances, perhaps killed by the Spaniards, perhaps by his own people. On 30 June, La Noche Triste ('the Sad Night'), the Spaniards and Tlaxcalans fled Tenochtitlan with heavy losses. A smallpox epidemic then swept the city, killing the new ruler Cuitlahuac in December. Weakened by disease, Tenochtitlan fell to Cortés and his allies in August 1521.
